*Cool wind moves through the rough grass around Alaric's boots.*

*The last thing that belongs to Earth is still there in memory—an old life, a world without visible mana, Classes, or this impossible second beginning. The present is different: the smell of soil and distant woodsmoke, an unfamiliar sky, and stone walls beyond the public road.*

*Alaric is already standing on an uncultivated roadside verge outside the nearby city. Cultivated fields and fenced holdings begin farther away. No one is close enough to have witnessed the instant of arrival.*

*The body is Human, healthy, and eighteen years old. Simple traveler's clothes are already being worn; a small pouch holding five silver rests at the belt. The memories are still from Earth.*

*A translucent interface opens across Alaric's vision.*

turns.input: *i walk towards the gate of the big city ahead*
turns.reply:
The road to Tidecross carried its morning already: two ox-carts bound the same direction, a woman with a basket of gulls' eggs, a boy driving geese with a willow switch. By the time the walls rose full height overhead — grey river-stone, salt-stained to the height of a man's chest — Alaric had been absorbed into the small, shuffling traffic of the road without anyone remarking on it.

The gate stood open. A queue had gathered at it, thin but slow, because the two men in Solmere's colors were stopping every third traveler for a look and a word. A brazier burned beside the gatehouse, more for the guards' hands than any signal; the wind off the water carried brine and tar and the cry of gulls fighting over something on the mole.

"Carts to the left lane, feet to the right," one of the guards called, bored to the bone. He had a lean face, a woollen cap, and a ledger under his arm that he clearly resented. "Toll's a copper a head, a copper per wheel. Names go in the book."

The line moved. Ahead, a tallow merchant argued his wheel-count — "It's one axle, Berold, one, the second axle's decorative, apparently" — while the guard named Berold wrote in his ledger with the patience of a man being paid by the hour. The other guard worked the line itself, eyes down each traveler: packs, weapons, faces. When his gaze reached Alaric it paused a moment on the longsword at his side, then moved on to the man behind him.

Somewhere inside the walls a bell rang twice, flat and unhurried, and the gulls answered it.

turns.input: *Once its my turn i hand over a copper to pay and wait for my change as i say* Name is Alaric
turns.reply:
"One copper, one name, one book entry." Berold held out a palm gone cracked at the thumb, took the coin, and bit it out of habit older than his interest in the job. "Alaric. Spell it."

He didn't wait for an answer before writing something that was probably close, tongue pressed to the corner of his mouth. "Alaric what? Family name, trade, whatever you'd call yourself." The quill hovered. "Half the men through here are 'just Alaric' by noon, I swear it on the book itself."

The lean guard drifted a step along the line and stopped — not in front of Alaric, but near enough. His eyes went to the sword again, then up. "Traveling light for a man carrying steel," he said, mild as milk. "Where'd you sleep last night?"

Behind them the tallow merchant snorted and drove his cart through, one axle and all. Berold ignored both of them, quill still waiting over the ledger, a smear of ink drying on his knuckle. The wind pushed the brazier's smoke sideways across the gate arch, and somewhere past the walls a ship's horn sounded, long and low.

turns.input: I dont have a family name but if you need one just put down Red *i say smiling politely* and i traveled light since i want to register with the adventurers guild so no reason to slow myself down.
turns.reply:
"Red." Berold wrote it without comment, though the quill paused long enough for him to glance up — the blond hair, the eyes — and something like a private joke settled into his face before he bent back to the book. "Alaric Red, foot traveler, one copper, paid." He flicked the register shut. "Through the arch, keep to the right of the market square, guildhall's the stone one with the antler over the door. Can't miss it unless you're blind or drunk."

The lean guard didn't move off, though. "Guild, is it." He said it the way a man says a word he's said too many times this season. "Lot of young blades through here wanting the guild lately. Ship crews hiring, dungeon freight coming up the coast — everybody smells the same money." He stepped aside at last, but his eyes stayed a moment longer than the toll required. "Sword's peace-bonded or not, I'll know the answer either way by sundown if there's trouble. Go on."

The arch swallowed the line behind them. Inside, Tidecross opened up all at once — cobbles slick with fish-water, a street of awnings strung with drying hake, porters hauling casks off a wagon, a woman crying oysters at two for a penny. The noise came down like weather after the open road.

And over the rooftops to the right, above the market square, an antler of iron jutted from a grey stone roof.

turns.input: *i walk inisde and follow the description as i walk to the guild building and go inside*
turns.reply:
"—three coppers a night, and you don't get to pick the room, Marda, that's the whole point of paying less—"

The argument belonged to a broad woman behind the guildhall's front counter, directed at nobody visible, or at somebody who'd already left. She had grey-streaked hair pinned back with what looked like a fishhook, and she was still talking at the empty doorway beside her when the door Alaric used let in the street noise behind him.

Inside was cooler, dimmer, and smelled of lamp oil, old paper, and something like wet dog. The stone floor had been swept but never won. Along the left wall stretched a great board pinned with notices — bounties on drawn charcoal wolves, a writ for "haulage, salt-cured dungeon hide, discreet inquiry," a bill for a lost ferry dog, reward one silver, "answers to Bristle." Two men in mud-caked leathers were bent over that board, arguing in low voices over a scrap of parchment between them. A third, younger, sat on the bench by the hearth with his arm in a splint, drinking something steaming and looking at nobody.

The broad woman turned on her stool and took Alaric in with one pass — sword, clothes, face, the face again.

"Guild business or asking directions to somewhere I'll pretend is guild business?" She pulled a ledger toward her across the counter, leaving a wet ring where a mug had stood on it. "If it's registration, sit-down's through that door, assessor's in with someone, and the fee's one silver whether you're Level one or Level forty, so think about that before you walk through it."

Behind her, the assessor's door stood closed. Muffled through it, someone was speaking in the patient, careful cadence of a man reciting terms he wanted remembered exactly.

turns.input: *i nod at her and walk to the door where i wait until im called in and go inside*
turns.reply:
The wait was short. The door opened from inside and a sea-worn man came out counting coins into a pouch, lips still moving over terms — "...third part on delivery, not before, you'll tell Harl it's third part or nothing..." — and gone past Alaric without a glance, still talking to a door already shut behind him.

"Next," said a voice from within. "Shut it behind you."

The assessor's room was small and honest: a desk scarred with knife-marks, a scale for weighing dungeon stone, a window letting in a bar of grey light and the smell of the harbor. The man behind the desk was old, thin as a gull, with ink on three fingers and a pair of half-moon spectacles pushed up into white hair.

"Sit." He pulled a blank form toward himself and dipped his pen. "Name. Age. Any prior guild membership, any other guild, any debt owed to a guild — and think before you answer the third one, because the clerks in Goldharbor have long memories and longer lists." He looked up over the form, and his eyes went briefly to the red ones, then back down, unremarked. "Weapon skill — sword, I see. Anything else? Bow, axe, teeth? And last question, and don't lie on it: ever been inside a natural Dungeon before, yes or no."

The pen waited. Somewhere below the window, a cart wheel squealed past on the cobbles.

turns.reply:
"Warrior." The pen scratched it down. "Never been under. Fine. That's what the rank's for — keeps the fresh ones alive long enough to stop being fresh."

He held out a flat palm for the silver, weighed it between two fingers by habit, and dropped it into a drawer that needed oiling. Then he slid the form aside and pulled a slate-grey tablet from under the desk — smooth, palm-sized, dull as river stone.

"Hand on this. Don't squeeze it, don't pray over it, just hold it."

The tablet warmed, then dimmed.

"Rank F, Power. Guild Rank Novice." He scratched something onto a wooden tag and pushed it across the desk with the tablet — a thin card stamped with the antler, his name burned into the corner in a clerk's cramped hand. "Guild tag. Don't lose it, replacing it costs two silver and my patience, which is worth more. Contract board's through the front room. As a Novice you take Novice-rank writs and below — the board's marked, the ones above your reach are chalked red, and if I catch a Novice holding a red-chalk contract I don't fine you, I laugh at you, and then the Questholder laughs at you."

He took off the spectacles, breathed on them, polished them with his sleeve.

"One thing, since you said never been under. Tidecross has two dungeons in its books. The Sump, down by the marsh road — wet, shallow, good for a first walk if you go with people who've been. And the Wreck of the Karst Maiden, off the harbor bar — the Guild seals that one, don't let anyone talk you onto a boat for it, the payouts they whisper about are lies told by men short on crew." He put the spectacles back on. "First writ, take something boring. Boring pays the same as exciting until it doesn't."

Through the wall, the broad woman's voice rose again — "...because Bristle's been found, Dorn, that's why the bill's coming down, put it—"
